Press Release:



The Listeriosis outbreak has wreaked havoc across South Africa. Now with over 900 confirmed cases and 180 people dead including infants and children, the Health Department has finally made a breakthrough in finding the source of the deadly disease. As families come to terms with their devastating losses, could a major class action lawsuit be on the cards for those affected?


Script:


LISTERIOSIS 2
V/O: In January we brought you the story of South Africa's deadly listeriosis outbreak, the biggest in global history.
Lucia: The deli meats, the cold cuts, quite a number of outbreaks have occurred due to those. If it cannot be cooked, it should preferably just simply be avoided.
V/O: At the time there were 727 confirmed cases of this food-borne disease, and 61 people had already died. Authorities frantically tried to find the source. Intensive DNA testing narrowed the search by identifying the particular strain of Listeria causing the outbreak.
Juno: All of our human cases that we've done this whole genome sequencing on to date, 91% of them belong to a single strain, and that's our outbreak strain.
Lucia: The fact that it's ST6 in 91% of the cases actually means that it probably comes from a single source.
V/O: Last Sunday, there was a breakthrough. With 948 confirmed cases and 180 deaths, the Minister of Health, Dr Aaron Motsoaledi announced they had found the source at last.
Minister: The NICD called me at 12 'o clock last night and told me they've got results from the Enterprise facility, and that the outbreak strain ST6 has been confirmed in at least 16 environmental samples that were collected from this site.
Link: The Enterprise factory in Polokwane is the epicentre of the listeriosis outbreak. 180 people are dead, but that figure could rise
V/O: The processing plant in Polokwane produces polony and other ready-to-eat cold cuts, like Vienna sausages that are distributed country-wide. This factory, together with the Enterprise processing plant in Germiston, and the Rainbow Chicken processing plant in Sasolburg in the Free State were closed for further investigation. Dr Juno Thomas, from the National Institute of Communicable Diseases explains how they made the breakthrough.
Juno: On the 12th of January, a group of 9 children attending a small creche in Soweto were admitted to Chris Hani Baragwanath hospital.

V/O: An environmental health practitioner immediately interviewed the creche owner to find out what the children had eaten, and sampled food still in the fridge.

Juno: These samples included 2 different brands of polony. We confirmed that the isolate from the child as well as the isolates taken from the polony samples in the fridge belonged to the outbreak strain, the ST6.

V/O: On the 2nd of February, Dr Thomas accompanied a team, including 3 food safety experts from the WHO in Geneva, to the Polokwane factory for a site inspection.

Juno: The reception wasn't particularly welcoming. Environmental health practitioners from the district municipality had been denied access twice. So, there was a police presence when we arrived, just to facilitate entry, in case the management refused.

Devi: Why wouldn't they let the health inspectors in?

Juno: They claim they weren't sure if the health inspectors were who they said they were.

V/O: Every area of the facility was intensively sampled, as well as some of the polony and Vienna products.

Juno: In total over 340 samples were taken. 104 yielded Listeria monocytogenes - almost 30%. So, it shows there was extensive environmental contamination with Listeria. Of those 104, 28 are the outbreak strain.

V/O: But this is not enough evidence for Tiger Brands.

Journalist: So today on the 5th of March you take no responsibility for those who died?

Lawrence: There is no direct link with the deaths to our products that we're aware of at this point. Nothing.

V/O: CEO Lawrence MacDougall then contradicted himself, admitting they also found the outbreak strain of Listeria on the 14th of February.

Lawrence: I have told you we've had no evidence of any link. The government has told us there's a link between ST6 and the outbreak of the strain, and we found evidence on our site of ST6. That's the only link that exists at the moment.

Link: This is a PR disaster. Tiger Brands' first response was to deny any responsibility for the 180 fatalities. This flies in the face of solid, scientific evidence gathered by the National Department of Health.

Juno: Over 90% of patients developed disease from the outbreak strain ST6, and the same holds for patients who died. Now we have evidence from the factory that both the direct environment was contaminated with ST6, as well as polony product that were about to be put onto pallets and shipped out to the retail industry had listeria on the exterior casings and the little folds alongside the clips.

Richard: It's like a fingerprint, or the grooves on a bullet. It's the smoking gun, it's the thing that links their disease condition with the same bacteria found at the factory in Polokwane, not same in a kind of generic way, same in a very, very specific way.
V/O: Richard Spoor is a pioneering human rights lawyer, who successfully pursued class action lawsuits on behalf of miners suffering from asbestosis and silicosis.
Richard: To build a case against Tiger you need to establish - the tough one is proving causation - you've got to prove it's their food that poisoned these victims. But once you've established causation, you're home and dry. The Consumer Protection Act provides for strict liability for consumer products, so if you sell a product and that product is defective and it causes harm, you are strictly liable. We don't have to prove you're negligent, we don't have to prove that you act with intention, we just need to prove it was your product that caused the harm, and then you're liable.


V/O: Spoor is planning a class action lawsuit representing all the victims of the outbreak, including the late Sonette Clack, who miscarried in November, three weeks before dying of meningitis.
Tonja: While she was pregnant they had polony, not most of the time, but they had that a lot.
V/O: On Sunday Tiger Brands recalled all their processed meat products. Consumers were encouraged to return their polony, viennas and Russians to retailers nationwide for a full refund.
But at Polokwane Factory shop customers were let in one-by-one and were only paid for what they returned.
Voxpops: They put it on the scale, then they tell you how much you are going to get.
I spend more than 500, now they refund me 400.
All these people that are here are supposed to be at work, supposed to do whatever they would be doing. Now they are queueing for plus minus 5 hours. It's bad.
Viennas, polonies must go down!
Well this is the second day now that I'm standing in the line.
Devi: You've been here for 2 days?
For 2 days yes.
Devi: Why?
Granny: Because I can't wait longer. I've got to fetch my grandchildren.
Link: The day after the Enterprise factories were named as the culprits in the world's biggest listeriosis outbreak, Tiger Brands share price was down by 7%. That's a R5.6 billion drop in value.
V/O: By Friday the share price had dropped over 13% in a week, slicing off another R5 billion in value.
But any legal damages will probably be covered by insurance.
Richard: If you're in the food business you have insurance against precisely this kind of eventuality. The contract of insurance will prevent or preclude the company from admitting liability. So, if the company says we accept guilt, we are responsible, and they do that without the agreement of the insurance company, they will lose the benefit of the insurance claim, because it's up to the insurer to decide whether or not they are going to accept liability.

Devi: So, choosing not to apologise is actually understandable in the circumstances?
Richard: He doesn't really have a choice. For a CEO of a company to admit liability on something like this, he could be fired.
Link: Since Monday we've been trying to get an interview with Tiger Brands. They didn't respond. But when we arrived on their doorstep, they said nobody was available to speak to us.
V/O: On Friday night they emailed us stating
They acted in good faith and have co-operated with the Department, the NICD, and Ekurhuleni and Capricorn municipalities
Provided access to the facilities, shared results of their rigorous product testing, and been transparent about their findings
Amplified listeria testing in both facilities since December 2017
They are tested by leading retail chains and have micro-laboratories on-site
Detection of low levels of environmental listeria is normal
Appointed experts to discover the root cause of ST6 in Polokwane
It is premature to call the Polokwane facility the source
No DNA test results confirm ST6 in any Tiger Brand products
No proof links the unfortunate deaths with test results in relation to Enterprise.
V/O: There are now 967 confirmed cases of listeriosis, and the death toll has risen to 183.
Juno: We still have 30% of patients to follow up, and we can expect that anywhere between 20 and 30% of those patients have died, so the death rate will increase.
V/O: Potentially, another hundred victims could already have lost their lives.
